# How a Compiler Works: From Source Text to Machine Code

A compiler is a program that translates source code written in a high-level language into a lower-level representation—typically machine code or bytecode—that a computer can execute. The process is conventionally divided into a front end (which analyzes the source language) and a back end (which targets a specific machine architecture), with an intermediate representation (IR) bridging the two. Below is a detailed walkthrough of the major phases: lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis and type checking, IR construction, optimization, and code generation.

## 1. Lexical Analysis (Scanning)

The first stage converts a stream of characters into a stream of tokens. A lexer (scanner) reads the source text and groups characters into meaningful units: identifiers, keywords, numeric literals, string literals, operators, and punctuation. This is typically implemented either by hand-written code or by a lexer generator such as Lex/Flex, which compiles regular expressions into a deterministic finite automaton (DFA). The DFA recognizes the longest match for each token according to the language's lexical rules.
